analysis.one_liner: Bans pharmacy middlemen from hidden spread pricing and pharmacy clawbacks unless they fully disclose drug costs and fees.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill barring pharmacy middlemen from hidden markups and pharmacy clawbacks cleared the Senate Commerce Committee unanimously but died without ever getting a Senate floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers, or PBMs, are middlemen that sit between your health plan and the pharmacy. This bill would have made it illegal for a PBM to charge your plan more for a drug than it pays the pharmacy and keep the difference, and to arbitrarily claw back money from pharmacies or cut their reimbursements. PBMs could escape those bans only by passing 100% of drug discounts to the health plan and fully disclosing their costs, fees, and markups. It also would have required annual reports to the Federal Trade Commission, protected whistleblowers, and let the FTC and state attorneys general enforce the rules with penalties. The Senate Commerce Committee approved it on a bipartisan basis and put it on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People with prescription drug coverage, whose out-of-pocket costs and premiums are shaped by how PBMs price drugs behind the scenes; independent and community pharmacies, which bear clawbacks and below-cost reimbursements; and employers, unions, and government programs (Medicare, Medicaid, FEHB) that pay drug benefits and would finally see the full flow of rebates, fees, and markups. The FTC and state attorneys general would gain new enforcement powers.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it illegal for a PBM to charge a health plan more for a drug than it pays the pharmacy and pocket the difference — a practice called spread pricing.
It bars PBMs from arbitrarily or deceptively clawing back reimbursement payments from pharmacies, or from raising pharmacy fees to offset reimbursement changes ordered by the federal government.

It requires PBMs to report annually to the Federal Trade Commission how much they keep of the spread between plans and pharmacies, what fees and clawbacks they impose on pharmacies, and why drugs are moved to costlier formulary tiers.
It lets the FTC and state attorneys general enforce the rules, with civil penalties up to $1,000,000 per violation in addition to standard FTC Act penalties.

It protects whistleblowers at PBMs, health plans, manufacturers, and pharmacies from being fired or retaliated against for reporting violations, and voids arbitration agreements that would block those claims.

It orders a GAO study of the PBM market, including market shares of the ten largest PBMs, how rebates are divided among patients, payers, and PBMs, and whether formularies favor high-rebate drugs over cheaper alternatives.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers, which would lose the revenue they keep from spread pricing, pharmacy fees, and clawbacks unless they fully disclosed their books and passed through every discount. Insurers that own large PBMs would absorb much of that loss, and some of it could be passed back to plans as higher PBM service fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their insurers

drawbacks.text: The ban on spread pricing has a large exception: a PBM can keep these practices off the prohibited list simply by passing along 100% of price concessions and disclosing its costs, fees, and markups — so the bill works mainly through transparency rather than an outright ban, and its real-world impact depends on how much disclosure changes behavior.

The added civil penalty is capped at $1,000,000 per violation, an amount that is modest for large PBMs handling billions in annual drug claims, and courts must weigh mitigating factors in assessing it.
PBMs gain an affirmative defense for conduct that was 'nonpretextual and reasonably necessary' to protect patient safety or patient access, which gives defendants room to contest enforcement.

Compliance burden: every PBM would have to file detailed annual reports to the FTC and disclose contract-level pricing to every plan and pharmacy, an administrative cost that critics said could be passed through to health plans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the whole the benefits outweigh the costs: the bill targeted specific, well-documented pricing practices — spread pricing and clawbacks — that raise drug costs for plans and squeeze pharmacies, and it paired the ban with real enforcement tools and whistleblower protection. The honest drawbacks are design limits rather than flaws: the disclosure exception turns a ban into a transparency regime, the $1,000,000 penalty cap is small relative to the revenues at stake for multi-billion-dollar middlemen, and the patient-safety affirmative defense gives defendants a way to contest enforcement. It also would not have lowered any drug's price directly — savings depended on transparency actually changing negotiated prices.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill and it sat on the Senate's calendar of business, but no senator ever brought it up for a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Maria Cantwell introduced the bill on May 24, 2022, and it was referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
On June 22, 2022, the Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.

On December 14, 2022, the committee reported the bill to the full Senate with an amendment, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders — the list of bills waiting for floor time.
The bill carried eight cosponsors, seven of them Republicans, giving it bipartisan sponsorship rare for drug-pricing legislation.
No further action was taken: the Senate never voted on the bill, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large pharmacy benefit managers are better off: federal rules banning spread pricing, clawbacks, and opaque fees never took effect, so their existing business model continued unregulated.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with eight cosponsors, seven of them Republicans, and cleared the Senate Commerce Committee on a bipartisan basis; the deciding factor was not opposition on the merits but the bill never reaching the floor.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (a market dominated by a few large firms such as CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, and Optum Rx)
industries.note: The bill bans spread pricing and deceptive clawbacks, forces annual disclosure of what PBMs keep from plan-pharmacy differences, and adds FTC and state enforcement with penalties up to $1,000,000 per violation. PBMs avoid the prohibitions only by passing 100% of discounts to plans and disclosing their fees — giving up the opacity that is central to the business. The bill died, so none of this took effect.

Pharmacies are the bill's most direct beneficiaries: it bars PBMs from clawing back reimbursements or cutting pharmacy payments to offset federal reimbursement changes, and requires PBMs to report whether they treat their own affiliated pharmacies better than independents. These practices have pushed independent pharmacies to close or operate at a loss.

industries.industry: Health insurers, employers, and government health plans that pay drug benefits
industries.note: Plans and payers gain full disclosure of what PBMs charge, keep, and receive from manufacturers, plus a requirement that all rebates be passed through. That improves their negotiating position, though most large PBMs are owned by insurers, so the same companies sit on both sides of the transaction.

The bill does not regulate manufacturer pricing directly, but it requires reporting on whether PBMs moved drugs to costlier tiers at a manufacturer's request and discloses aggregate manufacturer payments to PBMs, which would expose rebate-driven formulary practices that protect high-rebate drugs.
